title: Kalki
tomorrow: someone online calls an old law book 'the Hindu rulebook.' is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the age Kalki is promised to: an age of stand-ins, with one door open, singing the name. Today, what comes after Kalki.

When a long guest leaves, a house smells different for a while: their shampoo in the bathroom, their snack in the pantry, and then, slowly, just home again. A smell can be the first thing that says a season has turned. In the Bhagavata, that's how the next age begins. Not with a trumpet, but with a scent on the wind. Once Kalki has done his work, a breeze moves across the earth carrying sandalwood, and the people who breathe it find their minds gone clear.
screen: `THE HOUSE SMELLS DIFFERENT.` → `NOT A TRUMPET.` → `SANDALWOOD ON THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the Bhagavata's telling. When Kalki has put down the robbers who ruled as kings, the people who remain are touched by a breeze carrying the fragrance of sandal paste from the Lord's own body, and their minds turn clear. Then the Krita age, the age of truth, begins again. The book even mentions two kings who have been waiting quietly in a village called Kalapa, ready to start the royal lines over. So Kalki isn't the end of the story. He's the hinge that swings the ages back to the start: Krita, Treta, Dvapara, Kali, and then Krita once more. Time here turns like a wheel, not an arrow, and an ending is also the place where something starts. Now step back and see the whole series these weeks have walked. A fish in the flood. A tortoise under the mountain. A boar lifting the earth. A man-lion at the doorway. A dwarf's strides. Rama with the axe, and Rama with the bow. Krishna. The Buddha, as the tradition tells him. And Kalki, still to come, opening the wheel's next turn. Age after age, Krishna said in the Gita; the ten forms are that line, told as a story. The weeks in the Puranas close here. Next comes a different kind of book, a dharma text, read with care and a critical eye.
screen: `A BREEZE WITH SANDALWOOD IN IT.` · `THE AGE OF TRUTH BEGINS AGAIN.` · `A WHEEL, NOT AN ARROW.` · `THE WHOLE SERIES, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `AN ENDING IS ALSO A START.`

segments.voice: If there's something with a scent near you, a spice jar, soap, a cup of tea, hold it close and breathe it in slowly, three times. Then set it down and keep breathing in the trace it leaves for the rest of the sit. If there's nothing nearby, notice the plain smell of the room you're in.
Kalki: the form whose work closes the Kali age, after which a sandal-scented breeze clears minds and the age of truth comes round again.
Keep this: Kalki, the hinge where the wheel turns and the age of truth comes round again. And with that, the Puranas are done.

howItsDone: Sandal paste is offered in Hindu worship and applied to images of the gods; the four ages and their turning are retold in Purana recitations.

chat.meaning: After Kalki, the Bhagavata's first sign of the new age is a sandal-scented breeze that clears minds. A scent can mark a turn.
